up.note: The randomised strengthening of the certificate complexity barrier: $\mathrm{Adv} \le \sqrt{\mathrm{C}^{0}\mathrm{C}^{1}}$ [SpalekSzegedy06, Zhang05] survives replacing certificates by fractional ones. The second step is $\sqrt{ab} \le \max(a,b)$ together with $\mathrm{FC} = \mathrm{fbs}$ (an equality of LPs, see \(\mathrm{FC}(f)\)). Totality is load-bearing. Off the promise the bound weakens to $\mathrm{Adv}(f) \le 2\sqrt{n \cdot \min\{\mathrm{FC}^{0},\mathrm{FC}^{1}\}}$ [ABIKPS17], which is no use when the promise makes both fractional certificate complexities constant -- \(\mathrm{COL}_n\) again. Combined with $\mathrm{fbs} \le \mathrm{Adv}^2$ (cell above) this pins the positive adversary inside a square: $\sqrt{\mathrm{fbs}} \le \mathrm{Adv} \le \mathrm{fbs}$, which is what makes How much do negative weights buy the adversary? a question about $\mathrm{Q}$ versus $\mathrm{fbs}$.

  • \(\mathrm{Adv}(\oplus_n) = \Theta(n) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{fbs}(\oplus_n)\big)\)

up.note: The certificate complexity barrier, recorded here in the coarse two-measure form the matrix can use; the sharp statement involves $\mathrm{C}^{0}$ and $\mathrm{C}^{1}$ separately and is written out under \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\) vs \(\mathrm{Adv}(f)\) above. The second inequality is just $\sqrt{ab}\le\max(a,b)$. This is the precise sense in which the positive adversary cannot see past certificates -- and the reason $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}$ exists. Boolean output only. The barrier is a statement about $0/1$-valued $f$, where "$\mathrm{C}^{0}$" and "$\mathrm{C}^{1}$" mean something; it does not survive a large output alphabet. \(\mathrm{OS}_n\) is the sharpest illustration: two queries $\{x_k = 0,\; x_{k+1} = 1\}$ pin down the answer, so the decision version has $\mathrm{C} = 2$, yet the $(n+1)$-valued reconstruction version has $\mathrm{Adv} \ge \tfrac{1}{\pi}\ln n$ [ChildsLee08]. That is why the $\mathrm{C}$ row is left blank on that page rather than filled in with the constant.

Boolean output only. The barrier is a statement about $0/1$-valued $f$, where "$\mathrm{C}^{0}$" and "$\mathrm{C}^{1}$" mean something; it does not survive a large output alphabet. \(\mathrm{OS}_n\) is the sharpest illustration: two queries $\{x_k = 0,\; x_{k+1} = 1\}$ pin down the answer, so the decision version has $\mathrm{C} = 2$, yet the $(n+1)$-valued reconstruction version has $\mathrm{Adv} \ge \tfrac{1}{\pi}\ln n$ [ChildsLee08]. Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{Adv}(\oplus_n) = \mathrm{C}(\oplus_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\)
    Every input of $\oplus_n$ is fully sensitive, so $\mathrm{C}=n$, and the basic adversary on the Hamming-distance-one relation already gives $n$. So the barrier is attained and the cell closes.

Recorded under partial because nothing in the barrier's proof uses totality -- and the promise setting is exactly where it hurts, since a property-testing promise can force both certificate complexities to $O(1)$ while $\mathrm{Q}$ is polynomially large. The total-function row inherits it.

facts: Certificate complexity barrier: $\mathrm{Adv}(f) \le \sqrt{\mathrm{C}^0(f)\,\mathrm{C}^1(f)}$ [SpalekSzegedy06, Zhang05]. Note it is the product that is capped: element distinctness has $\mathrm{C}^1 = 2$ but $\mathrm{C}^0 = n$, so the barrier only says $\mathrm{Adv} = O(\sqrt n)$. It is the property-testing promise problems, with both certificate complexities $O(1)$, on which the positive adversary collapses to $\mathrm{Adv} = O(1)$ — \(\mathrm{COL}_n\), \(\mathrm{SIMON}_n\) [HoyerSpalek05].
Sharper: $\mathrm{Adv}(f) \le \sqrt{\mathrm{RC}^0(f)\,\mathrm{RC}^1(f)}$, the randomized-certificate version of the barrier [KulkarniTal16].
For total search problems $\mathrm{Adv}$ can be exponentially smaller than $\widetilde{\deg}$ [BenDavidKundu24search].

up.note: The positive-weight adversary can never beat the polynomial method by more than a square, even on promise problems. This is the cleanest way to see why the Ambainis-Belovs separation had to use negative weights: \(\mathrm{TSAT}_n\) has $\deg = 9$, hence $\widetilde{\deg} \le 9$, hence $\mathrm{Adv} = O(1)$, against $\mathrm{Q} = \widetilde\Omega(n^{1/3})$. Compare the certificate barrier under \(\mathrm{Adv}(f)\) vs \(\mathrm{C}(f)\): that one bites on property-testing promises, this one bites on low-degree ones.
